sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force / RFC Editor
sources.name: RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics
sources.role: HTTP method/status/representation/validator and conditional-request semantics contract
verified_facts: RFC 9110 defines the common architecture, terminology and semantics shared by HTTP versions.
HTTP status codes describe the result of applying request semantics; a successful status does not define application-specific data quality.
Entity tags are opaque validators associated with selected representations and can be used by conditional requests.
semantic_limits: A 200 or 206 response does not prove source authority, complete distribution identity, exact parcel geometry or numeric accuracy.
An ETag is a representation validator and must not be treated as a cryptographic digest unless an independently specified digest contract is also verified.
Content negotiation and representation metadata must not substitute for immutable source version, exact bytes, CRS, vertical datum, units and provenance.

sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force / RFC Editor
sources.name: RFC 9111 — HTTP Caching
sources.role: cache storage, freshness, validation, age and stale-response reuse contract
verified_facts: An HTTP cache stores response messages for reuse when satisfying later equivalent requests.
A fresh stored response can be reused without contacting the origin server for validation.
A stale response can sometimes be reused or refreshed according to cache directives, validators and availability rules.
semantic_limits: Cache freshness means reusable under HTTP rules; it does not prove that the data is the newest canonical publication.
Age, Expires and max-age values do not establish source authority, terrain currency or measurement accuracy.
A cached response must not create a business row without pinned distribution identity, byte integrity, exact geometry and measurement receipts.

sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force / RFC Editor
sources.name: RFC 9112 — HTTP/1.1
sources.role: HTTP/1.1 message syntax, parsing, body-length determination and connection-delimited framing contract
verified_facts: RFC 9112 specifies HTTP/1.1 message syntax, parsing, connection management and message framing.
Message body length is determined by ordered rules involving request method, status, Transfer-Encoding, Content-Length and connection closure.
A close-delimited response cannot distinguish successful message completion from a network interruption.
semantic_limits: Successful HTTP parsing or framing does not prove a cryptographic digest, source authority or scientific correctness.
Connection closure must not be treated as a complete-download receipt for a source object.
Content-Length or chunk framing proves transport boundaries only and must not replace exact source version, geometry, CRS, datum and method evidence.

sources.publisher: Internet Engineering Task Force / RFC Editor
sources.name: RFC 9113 — HTTP/2
sources.role: HTTP/2 binary framing, stream state, multiplexing, header compression and END_STREAM contract
verified_facts: HTTP/2 is an optimized expression of HTTP semantics using binary frames and multiplexed streams.
Frames are associated with streams and DATA or HEADERS frames can carry END_STREAM to indicate no further frames from that sender.
Stream errors and connection errors have defined scopes and can terminate individual streams or the connection.
semantic_limits: END_STREAM proves protocol-level stream completion only; it does not prove that the selected source object is complete, authoritative or correct.
Multiplexing and header compression improve transport behavior and do not establish source provenance or byte integrity.
A completed HTTP/2 exchange must not become parcel-height evidence without exact bytes, digest, geometry, CRS, vertical datum, units, method and execution receipts.
